title: Regularisation for Deep Networks
oneLiner: Regularisation is everything we do to stop a powerful network from memorising its training data, so that it works well on data it has never seen.

what.html:
Regularisation means adding constraints so a model can't become too complex and memorise its training data. Some are explicit (a penalty on large weights), some are built into the network (dropout, normalisation layers), and some are about how we train (early stopping, data augmentation). This session also covers good weight initialisation, which keeps deep networks trainable in the first place.

Everyday versionA student who memorises last year's exam answers scores 100% on that paper and fails the new one. A good teacher varies the practice questions, makes the student explain without notes, and stops drilling once mock-exam marks stop improving. Those are data augmentation, dropout and early stopping.

why.html:
• Networks with millions of weights can memorise entire datasets: perfect training accuracy, poor test accuracy.
  • The more powerful the model, the stronger the constraints it needs to generalise.
  • Very deep networks also suffer from signals that shrink or blow up from layer to layer; initialisation and normalisation fix that.
  • Regularisation may lower training accuracy a little, but it raises the accuracy that matters: on new data.

how.title: Spot overfitting and choose a family
how.html: Training error keeps falling while validation error starts rising: the model is now learning noise. Regularisers come in two families: explicit (weight penalties L1/L2, structural tricks like dropout) and implicit (training procedures like early stopping, normalisation layers).

how.title: Know the deep-network troublemakers
how.html: Backpropagation multiplies one factor per layer. Factors below 1 make the gradient vanish (early layers stop learning); factors above 1 make it explode (NaN losses). Layers also keep seeing their input distribution change as earlier layers learn (covariate shift). Fixes: careful initialisation, normalisation, clipping and residual connections.

how.title: Start the weights at the right size
how.html: All zeros: every neuron is identical forever. Too small: the signal fades. Too large: it explodes. The fix is to scale the random weights to the number of inputs: Xavier (variance 2/(inputs + outputs)) for tanh/sigmoid, He (variance 2/inputs) for ReLU, which switches off about half its inputs.

how.title: Penalise big weights: L2 and L1
how.html: Add λ × (size of the weights) to the loss. L2 (sum of squares) shrinks every weight a little each step, which is why it's called weight decay. L1 (sum of absolute values) pushes unimportant weights all the way to zero, so it also selects features. Choose λ by checking validation performance, for example with k-fold cross-validation.

how.title: Dropout: train many thinned networks
how.html: During training, switch off each hidden unit at random with probability p, a fresh choice every step. No unit can rely on a particular partner, so features become more robust. At test time, use every unit and make sure the average signal matches (frameworks scale during training, so nothing changes at test time). Variants drop connections, image blocks or attention weights.

how.title: Normalise inside the network
how.html: Batch norm rescales each feature to mean 0, variance 1 using the statistics of the current mini-batch, then lets the network learn its own scale γ and shift β. It allows higher learning rates and adds a little useful noise, but it needs reasonably large batches and keeps running averages for test time. Layer norm normalises across the features of each sample instead, so it works with any batch size and is the standard in RNNs and Transformers.

how.title: Stop at the right moment
how.html: Watch validation loss each epoch. When it hasn't improved for a set number of epochs (patience, typically 5–20), stop and go back to the best saved weights. It's free, automatic, and acts much like an L2 penalty.

how.title: Make more training data
how.html: Flip, crop, rotate, recolour or add noise to images; swap synonyms or back-translate text. The label stays the same, so the model sees more variety. Mixup blends two images and their labels; CutMix pastes a patch of one into the other. Split the data first and augment only the training set.

how.title: Pick a recipe and tune it
how.html: Small tabular data: L2 + early stopping + cross-validation. Small image data: careful augmentation. Text: dropout + layer norm. Big data and compute: the full suite. Tune the learning rate first, then the penalty strength, dropout rates, batch size and augmentation. Watch the gap between training and validation accuracy.

how.title: Match the architecture and avoid classic mistakes
how.html: CNNs: augmentation, batch norm, DropBlock. RNNs: the same dropout mask at every time step, gradient clipping, layer norm. Transformers: attention dropout, layer norm, label smoothing, warmup. Classic mistakes: leaving dropout on at test time, putting batch norm before the convolution, keeping the same learning rate after adding strong regularisation, augmenting before the train/validation split.

demo.html: Pick ReLU and look at layer 10: small weights shrink the signal to almost nothing, large weights blow it up, Xavier slowly fades it, and He keeps it steady. Switch to tanh: now Xavier is the right choice and large weights just saturate every unit at ±1. Increase the number of layers to see how quickly bad initialisation compounds.

example.html:
Batch norm on the batch [10, 12, 8, 14]: mean 11, variance 5, normalised to −0.45, 0.45, −1.34, 1.34, then scaled by γ = 2 and shifted by β = 3 to 2.1, 3.9, 0.32, 5.68. Layer norm on one sample [2, 8, 4, 10]: mean 6, variance 10, normalised to −1.26, 0.63, −0.63, 1.26. Mixup with λ = 0.7 gives the label 0.7 cat + 0.3 dog.

Supplementary A clinic trains an X-ray classifier on 2,000 images and hits 100% training accuracy but 71% on new scans. Adding flips, small rotations and brightness changes, dropout before the classifier and early stopping lifts validation accuracy, while vertical flips are left out because they don't occur in real scans.

misunderstandings: It usually lowers it slightly; the goal is better accuracy on unseen data.
Dropout should stay on when making predictions.
Switch it off at inference (model.eval()); otherwise predictions are random.
Initialising all weights to zero is a safe, neutral start.
Every neuron then computes and learns the same thing; random, properly scaled weights are needed.
Batch norm works the same with any batch size.
With tiny batches its statistics are noisy, and with batch size 1 it breaks; use layer or group norm.
Too much makes the model underfit: training and validation loss both stay high.
takeaways: Regularisation constrains complexity: explicit (L1/L2, dropout) and implicit (early stopping, normalisation, augmentation).
Initialise with Xavier for tanh/sigmoid and He for ReLU to avoid vanishing or exploding signals.
L2 shrinks weights (weight decay); L1 zeroes them (feature selection); choose λ on validation data.
Dropout trains random sub-networks; batch norm (CNNs, big batches) and layer norm (RNNs, Transformers) stabilise training.
Early stopping, data augmentation (Mixup, CutMix), sensible defaults per architecture, and monitoring the train–val gap complete the toolkit.
thirty: Regularisation stops a high-capacity network from memorising its training data, trading a little bias for much lower variance. Explicit methods add a penalty, such as L2 weight decay, which shrinks weights, or L1, which drives some to zero, or change the structure, such as dropout, which randomly removes units during training. Implicit methods change the training: early stopping restores the weights with the best validation loss, and data augmentation, including Mixup and CutMix, enlarges the training set. Deep networks also need Xavier or He initialisation so signals neither vanish nor explode, and normalisation: batch norm across the batch for CNNs, layer norm across features for RNNs and Transformers. Choose techniques by data size, architecture and compute, tune the learning rate first, and watch the gap between training and validation curves.
